Calculate the determinant $|\hat{\bm{\Sigma}}| = \hat{\Sigma}_{11}\hat{\Sigma}_{22} - \hat{\Sigma}_{12}^2$ [S2].

The source text explicitly defines the inverse covariance matrix decomposition in Equation (5) as: $a =  rac{ at{Sigma}_{22}}{| at{ Sigma}|}$, $b = - rac{ at{Sigma}_{12}}{| at{ Sigma}|}$, and $c =  rac{ at{Sigma}_{11}}{| at{ Sigma}|}$. In linear algebra, for a 2x2 matrix $ at{Sigma} =  egin{bmatrix}  at{Sigma}_{11} &  at{Sigma}_{12} &  at{Sigma}_{12} &  at{Sigma}_{22}  end{bmatrix}$, the inverse is given by $ egin{bmatrix}  at{Sigma}_{22} & - at{Sigma}_{12} & - at{Sigma}_{12} &  at{Sigma}_{11}  end{bmatrix}  rac{1}{det( at{Sigma})}$. Comparing the coefficients from the source text with the standard formula, it follows that $| at{ Sigma}| =  at{Sigma}_{11} at{Sigma}_{22} -  at{Sigma}_{12}^2$. Thus, the evidence supports the claim.

Analytic-Splatting is a rendering method that replaces the point-sampling of 2D Gaussians in 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) with an analytical approximation of the integral of the Gaussian signal over the pixel window area [S2].

The claim states that Analytic-Splatting replaces the point-sampling of 2D Gaussians in 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) with an analytical approximation of the integral of the Gaussian signal over the pixel window area. Source [S2] explicitly supports this in multiple places: 1) The abstract states, 'we present Analytic-Splatting, which analytically approximates the Gaussian integral within the 2D-pixel window area to better capture the intensity response of each pixel.' 2) The introduction contrasts it with 3DGS, noting that 'Rather than discrete sampling in 3DGS... we analytically approximate the integral within each pixel area.' 3) The notes confirm that the method 'replaces the point-sampling of 2D Gaussians in 3DGS with an analytical approximation of the integral of the Gaussian signal over the pixel window area.' All facts in the claim are present in the evidence.
